title: The First Public Atheist Was a Country Priest Who Didn't Dare Publish
dek: Meslier wrote the Testament denying God's existence but dared only to copy three manuscripts for posterity; Bayle used skepticism to show that religious questions exceed reason, and therefore no one has the right to persecute others in the name of faith.
why: This episode opens the "history of atheism" series; the information density is moderate, but Bayle's argument for toleration is a complete chain worth hearing closely.
who: Listeners interested in the history of early modern atheism and religious toleration, especially those who want to understand how Bayle defended toleration with skepticism.
skip: The opening chitchat about the show's 500-episode milestone and future plans can be skipped.

points.h: Five hundred episodes without a single public atheist
points.body: The show has reached nearly five hundred episodes without ever featuring a thinker who publicly declared himself an atheist. The ancients who were occasionally accused of atheism, on closer inspection, mostly held only unorthodox understandings of divinity, such as the Epicureans. The only ancient case that really stands up is the sophist Diagoras, but his writings are lost. The author therefore proposes: if there really is a clearly atheist history of philosophy, its European starting point is probably around the turn of the eighteenth century.

points.h: A priest writes a manuscript denying God
points.body: Meslier (Jean Meslier) was an obscure country priest of blameless life, yet he left behind a Testament that fiercely attacked Christianity and denied God's existence. He said he had accepted holy orders to please his parents and had always loathed performing those idolatrous and superstitious masses. He dismantled the faith from several angles: there is no reason to prefer Christianity to other religions; Christians are required to believe absurd doctrines that other religions lack, such as the Eucharist; the quarrels and violence among Christians themselves show precisely the danger of blind belief; the Old Testament endorses animal sacrifice and absurdly claims that God chose the Jews.

points.h: The problem of evil is his main weapon against God
points.body: Meslier was a rationalist who claimed his arguments relied only on the "light of natural reason," and that this light led him to the conclusion that God does not exist at all. His chief argument is the problem of evil; he says ironically that Christians call God a father, yet this father abandons his children to every kind of suffering and evil. He had utter contempt for arguments for God's existence, especially against Fénelon: if perfect things need a creator, then does this perfect creator not also need a creator, leading to an infinite regress; since the physical universe plainly exists, why not stop there instead of positing an invisible cause.

points.h: He dared not publish in his lifetime, and copied only three
points.body: Why has no one heard of this man, why was he not arrested or even executed? Two questions, one answer: Meslier was bold and fearless, but not bold enough to publish these heretical thoughts in his lifetime. In his later years he copied three manuscripts of the Testament for posterity, claimed not to care about posthumous reputation, and ended by writing that he was "almost nothing, and would soon be nothing." He did want to be read; the text often calls on readers to abandon superstition and to resist tyranny closely bound up with religion. He held that the idea of God was originally invented by rulers to oppress others more effectively.

points.h: Religion and politics prop each other up, and he also advocated communism
points.body: Meslier wrote that religion supports political rule, however vicious it may be; political rule in turn supports religion, however false it may be. He went further and advocated communism, imagining a society in which all property is held in common, modeled on Plato's Republic. Thus the charges against him would include sedition in addition to blasphemy and heresy. A few years after his death, copies began to circulate secretly; Voltaire published excerpts in 1761 but avoided the most seditious parts. This cautious and incomplete reception meant that Meslier failed to spark the political and conscientious revolution he wanted.

points.h: His arguments were not new to contemporary readers
points.body: The author suspects Meslier's arguments would only have shocked readers, not shaken their faith. For such anti-religious arguments had long been considered over and over, precisely in order to refute them. What is special about the Testament is the emotional intensity and its political agenda; but as for the arguments about religion and God, it resembles a scholastic treatise with only the hypothetical objections kept and the replies deleted. The theologians Meslier despised would, at least in their own view, have had little difficulty meeting his challenge.

points.h: Another anonymous atheist work, nine hundred pages
points.body: A few decades before Meslier, the Theophrastus Redivivus, written in 1659, likewise circulated only in a few manuscript copies and was not published until the early 1980s. Its title page lists Diagoras, the Epicureans, Sextus Empiricus, and also Protagoras—who said he could not know whether the gods exist, which strictly speaking is agnosticism rather than atheism. Strangely, the theists Plato and Aristotle are also listed on the title page; the book explains that they too were really atheists who merely concealed their true beliefs under a veil of dogma. This anonymous author was evidently a firm atheist as well; he opposed faith to natural reason and said that in a fair debate, theologians would have no chance if they used only purely rational premises that philosophers would accept.

points.h: A pious frame wraps nine hundred pages of atheism
points.body: Unlike Meslier, this author placed his lengthy atheistic discussion inside a pious frame: brief statements at the beginning and end say that these arguments are only meant to enable learned theologians to refute them. But this looks like mere lip service, since these few pages of religious piety are sandwiched between roughly nine hundred pages of atheistic argument. Because both Meslier and the Theophrastus Redivivus were little known at the time, the title of the first known atheist in early modern Europe probably goes to Matthias Knutzen, who in 1674 distributed anti-religious pamphlets in Germany, even handing them out in churches and at the university in Jena.

points.h: Bayle: a non-public atheist with greater influence
points.body: Knutzen was therefore written into Bayle's dictionary. Bayle did not publicly agree with Knutzen, but noted that alongside his atheistic views Knutzen affirmed solid ethical principles, showing that unbelief does not necessarily lead to immorality. As for Bayle's own position on religious belief or unbelief, it is far more obscure than that of the public atheists, but partly for that very reason it spread and influenced far more widely. As a result, Bayle's importance in the history of atheism is at least as great as that of Meslier, Knutzen, and the authors of those anonymous irreverent works, even though Bayle himself very likely—doubts notwithstanding—remained a believing Christian.

points.h: A community made up entirely of atheists
points.body: In the earlier Miscellaneous Thoughts on the Comet of 1681, Bayle criticized people's reaction to the comet's appearance the previous year, which many took as some kind of omen. Bayle said this superstition was worse than atheism. He went on to observe that a community made up entirely of atheists would probably be no less harmonious or moral than a religious community. He explained that pity, temperance, kindly dispositions, and so on do not come from knowing that a God exists, but from a certain temperament, together with education, self-interest, the desire for praise, an instinct of reason, or similar motives—motives that exist in atheists just as in anyone else.

points.h: Atheists can do good just as Christians can
points.body: Bayle's line of thought here resembles that of Catholic moralists such as La Rochefoucauld, but he drew a conclusion they evidently did not notice: since people often do good from considerations such as reputation rather than religious belief, atheists should be able to do good just as religious people do. Bayle may have been less cynical than the French moralists; he mentions an instinct of reason, not only self-interest; elsewhere in the Comet he seems to accept that unbelievers may also perform genuinely altruistic acts. But in the first clarification of the dictionary, Bayle retreats to a position more like La Rochefoucauld's, saying that when ancient pagans and atheists did good, they were not truly virtuous but merely acted well out of self-love.

points.h: Executed criminals always seem to have been believers
points.body: In the clarification Bayle says quietly that in the dictionary he has always tried, where possible, to mention the wicked deeds of atheists, but that the historical evidence for such deeds is scarce—of course, mainly because there were so few atheists to discuss in the first place. But he adds provocatively that criminals executed for monstrous crimes always seem to have been believers. From Bayle's other works it is clear that for him moral conscience springs from reason rather than faith: the principles of good conduct are universal and need not rest on a grasp of God. Just as atheists have no trouble doing mathematical proofs, they can also do what is right.

points.h: Arguing for religious toleration from a Bible verse
points.body: Like Meslier, Bayle was enraged by violence among Christians, but instead of using it directly to reject religion, he argued passionately for the value of religious toleration. Central here is his philosophical commentary on one biblical sentence: Jesus says people should be compelled to enter through the door, lest they be shut out. Augustine and others interpreted this to mean that the church may use coercion to force people to join and take part in the true religion. Bayle opposed this; like Meslier, he pointed to the diversity of religions: all believers think their own religion is true, and they can all equally think they have reason to impose their faith on others—a recipe for disaster, exactly the kind of disaster Europe was then suffering. Bayle's own brother died in imprisonment under religious persecution, so this was never a theoretical question for him.

points.h: If Calvinism happened to be right, could it persecute?
points.body: There is an obvious objection to Bayle: suppose Calvinist Protestants happened to be right, and not only Christianity is true but Calvinism is also the correct interpretation of Christian doctrine. Then Calvinists would have reason to persecute others, hoping to win them back to the truth; after all, those people's salvation hangs by a thread, and leaving them in error and sin would even be unforgivable negligence. Bayle's answer relies on his concept of moral conscience: everyone at all times has an unconditional obligation to do what he believes to be morally right. He borrows a Montaigne-style example: you see a little girl about to fall into a well, and conscience tells you to lunge and push her away, even at the cost of slightly injuring her. It turns out it was not a well at all, only a paddling pool decorated to look like one, and the child was perfectly safe; but because you did not know, your obligation to push the child away was just as real.

Bayle argues from this: if persecuting others for the true religion is right, then anyone who believes his own religion to be true is obliged to persecute others for it, whether or not that religion is actually true. This is absurd, because it means Catholics and Protestants were both fulfilling obligations and acting rightly when they persecuted each other, and so were Muslims persecuting Christians. To this one might reply: we do have an obligation to follow the judgment of conscience, but when the judgment is clearly mistaken, it is less credible that the obligation still holds. Back to the paddling-pool example: if I inferred it was a well merely because there was a bucket beside it, ignoring that it was bright pink plastic and had an inflatable giraffe floating in it, then it was my fault for jumping to conclusions, and my supposed obligation is weakened by my carelessness in forming the belief. In scholastic terms, one is excused for error only under "invincible ignorance"; and in religious matters ignorance is not unavoidable—we can find the right answer, and we are obliged to look for it.

points.h: Bayle's skepticism: reason cannot adjudicate religion
points.body: It is precisely here that Bayle's skeptical method becomes crucial. His dictionary returns again and again to the difficulty of establishing truth in religious matters. A typical example is his treatment of the problem of evil raised by Meslier. Bayle discusses this problem in several parts of the dictionary, including the entry on Manichaeism and one of the closing clarifications. He boldly suggests that the Manichaeans had compelling reasons to reject belief in a single all-good God and instead to posit a second supernatural power, a "counter-God" responsible for evil. Bayle says one can give what he calls an a priori argument for monotheism, namely that purely rational considerations point to a single God; but the a posteriori evidence of suffering in the world strongly supports the Manichaean view.

points.h: Reason has no standing in the religious domain
points.body: Bayle seems to think this is in effect an argumentative stalemate that reason cannot resolve. If we still accept monotheism, it must be out of faith in revelation. As he says in the clarification, it is impossible to resolve the difficulties raised by philosophers, and therefore a dispute using only the light of nature will always end badly for the theologians, who will be forced to give ground and take refuge under the protection of supernatural light. This example shows that for Bayle religious matters lie beyond the scope of natural reason, and reason has no standing in this domain at all. Then we certainly cannot be obliged to discover the truth: in religious matters we grope in the dark, so this ignorance, even if not invincible, is at least excusable.

points.h: What about the person whose conscience tells him to persecute
points.body: This helps Bayle deal with another problem often thought to arise from his theory of toleration: if someone's conscience tells him he ought to persecute, does Bayle's theory not imply that he is fulfilling an obligation? Bayle notices this "conscientious persecutor" problem and tries to escape it. He says that, paradoxical as it sounds, there are cases in which we do have an obligation to do wrong: it is wrong to knock over a child playing quietly by the paddling pool, but if the pool looks like a well, I am still obliged to do so; likewise a judge who condemns an innocent man does wrong, but if the evidence seems clearly to point to his guilt, he is still obliged to condemn. The conscientious persecutor seems to be in this situation, obliged to oppress others even though oppression is evil.

points.h: The evil of persecution is plainly evident
points.body: This may already be enough for Bayle, because it shows that the persecutor really is doing wrong. He would be caught in a dilemma: to persecute is a sin, and to persecute against conscience is also a sin. But the key point is that Bayle can say that, unlike the mysteries of religion, the evil of persecution is plainly evident. He has just given a very straightforward argument for why persecution inevitably leads to mutual violence without justification. So anyone who has reflected on this, especially anyone who has read Bayle, ought to abandon the judgment of conscience that tells them to oppress others, and if they have not done so, they are to blame.
